query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex Ti-V-Nb-Ta high-entropy alloy, trace interstitial impurities (oxygen and nitrogen) initially provide solid-solution strengthening but, upon high-temperature aging, diffuse toward grain boundaries together with Ti to form brittle α-Ti precipitates. This precipitation drains the adjacent matrix leading to the formation of precipitate‐free zones (PFZs) that lack the interstitial strengthening, thereby creating local sites of reduced toughness that promote brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase Ti-V-Nb-Ta high-entropy alloy with low, uniformly distributed levels of oxygen and nitrogen interstitials.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal aging (e.g., 700°C for up to 40 days) to trigger impurity diffusion and phase segregation.
generation.conditions: Aging under high-temperature service conditions relevant to demanding engineering applications, with subsequent mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation and tensile tests) at room temperature and/or elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of grain boundary α-Ti precipitates and adjacent precipitate-free zones (PFZs) depleted in impurity interstitials.
generation.mechanism: During aging, the interstitial oxygen and nitrogen migrate toward grain boundaries with Ti, stabilizing the brittle α-Ti phase there. This leads to a compositional gradient where the matrix adjacent to the grain boundary is depleted (PFZ), resulting in a local loss of solid-solution strengthening. The consequent contrast in mechanical properties between the strengthened matrix and the brittle grain boundaries fosters intergranular brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-homogenized baseline, aged samples will show detectable α-Ti precipitates at grain boundaries with adjacent PFZs, a measurable decrease in nanoindentation hardness (e.g., a ~16% drop observed over aging), and an increased propensity for brittle (intergranular) fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.baseline: A homogenized sample with uniform interstitial distribution and a single-phase BCC microstructure exhibiting both high strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to compositionally complex alloys with trace interstitial impurity levels (up to about 3 at.% oxygen/nitrogen) aged under service-like temperatures. It may not hold if impurity concentrations significantly exceed these levels or if additional alloying elements alter the diffusion or phase stability behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship among PFZ width, precipitate density, and the degree of embrittlement remains not fully defined. Moreover, the threshold impurity level and aging duration necessary to trigger significant brittleness could vary with slight compositional or processing changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-V-Nb-Ta HEA samples: one with rigorously controlled low interstitial content and a second with deliberately elevated oxygen and nitrogen levels within the trace range. Subject both sets to a series of thermal aging treatments (e.g., 700°C for 10, 20, and 40 days). Perform microstructural analysis (transmission electron microscopy and energy-dispersive spectroscopy) to quantify the formation of grain boundary α-Ti precipitates and measure PFZ widths. Conduct mechanical testing (nanoindentation for hardness and tensile tests for fracture mode analysis) to assess ductility and fracture characteristics.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and precipitate identification (TEM/EDS)
Nanoindentation hardness values before and after aging
Fracture surface analysis to evaluate intergranular versus transgranular failure modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aging does not lead to the formation of significant grain boundary α-Ti precipitates and adjacent PFZs, or if the expected decrease in hardness and shift to intergranular brittle fracture are not observed compared to the as-homogenized baseline (especially in samples with elevated interstitial levels), then the hypothesized mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The CALPHAD calculations indicate that oxygen can substantially affect the phase stability in Ti-V-Nb-Ta. In the absence of oxygen, equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta is predicted to exhibit a single-phase BCC structure, while trace levels of oxygen facilitate the formation of the α-Ti phase at the aging temperature, consistent with oxygen’s role as an α-stabilizer in Ti alloy (). As nitrogen is also an α-stabilizer in Ti alloys, it may play a similar role to oxygen in facilitating the formation of α-Ti phase in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta. Grain boundary α-Ti precipitates are observed to nucleate initially, followed by the formation of intragranular precipitates and the emergence of PFZs adjacent to the grain boundaries. The experimental characterization and equilibrium phase calculations lead to the inference that the formation of PFZ in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta system is the result of diffusion of Ti and major interstitials (O and N) to grain boundaries, with subsequent formation of nitrogen- and oxygen-rich α-Ti precipitates at the aging temperature.
